questions.prompt: A \(0.40\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle moves at \(5.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) perpendicular to a radius \(0.30\,\mathrm{m}\). Find \(L\) about the origin.
A disk has \(I=0.25\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}\) and \(\omega=16\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). Find its angular momentum about its axle.
A particle moves directly away from the origin. What is its angular momentum about the origin?
questions.answer:
It is zero because \(\vec r\) and \(\vec p\) are parallel:
\[
\vec L=\vec r\times\vec p=\vec0
\]

questions.prompt: If \(\vec r\) points along \(+\hat\imath\) and \(\vec p\) points along \(+\hat\jmath\), what direction is \(\vec L\)?
questions.answer:
\[
\hat\imath\times\hat\jmath=\hat k
\]
So \(\vec L\) points in the \(+\hat k\) direction.

questions.prompt: A \(2.0\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle is at \(\vec r=3\hat\imath+1\hat\jmath\,\mathrm{m}\) and has velocity \(\vec v=4\hat\jmath\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find \(L_z\).
A net torque of \(6.0\,\mathrm{N\,m}\) acts for \(2.5\,\mathrm{s}\) along a fixed axis. Find the change in angular momentum.
A particle has \(m=0.20\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(r=0.50\,\mathrm{m}\), \(v=8.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the angle between \(\vec r\) and \(\vec v\) is \(30^\circ\). Find \(L\).
A wheel's angular momentum changes from \(3.0\) to \(11.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}\) in \(4.0\,\mathrm{s}\). Find the average external torque.

A particle moves in the plane with \(\vec r(t)=bt\,\hat\imath+c\,\hat\jmath\) and \(\vec v=b\,\hat\imath\), where \(b\) and \(c\) are constants. Find \(\vec L\) about the origin and interpret why it is constant.
questions.answer:
The momentum is
\[
\vec p=m\vec v=mb\,\hat\imath
\]
Then
\[
\vec L=\vec r\times\vec p=(bt\,\hat\imath+c\,\hat\jmath)\times mb\,\hat\imath
\]
\[
\vec L=-mbc\,\hat k
\]
It is constant because the particle moves in a straight line with constant perpendicular distance \(c\) from the origin.

questions.prompt: A disk with \(I=0.40\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}\) spins at \(20\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). A constant external torque of \(2.0\,\mathrm{N\,m}\) acts opposite the spin for \(3.0\,\mathrm{s}\). Find the final angular momentum and angular speed.
questions.answer:
Initial angular momentum:
\[
L_i=I\omega_i=0.40(20)=8.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}
\]
The torque impulse is opposite the spin:
\[
\Delta L=-\tau\Delta t=-2.0(3.0)=-6.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}
\]
\[
L_f=2.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}
\]
\[
\omega_f=\frac{L_f}{I}=\frac{2.0}{0.40}=5.0\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}
\]

questions.prompt: A particle moves under a central force \(\vec F=f(r)\hat r\). Show that its angular momentum about the force centre is conserved, and state what this implies about the plane of motion.
questions.answer:
For a central force,
\[
\vec F=f(r)\hat r
\]
The torque about the force centre is
\[
\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F
\]
Since \(\vec F\) is parallel or antiparallel to \(\vec r\),
\[
\vec\tau=\vec0
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{d\vec L}{dt}=\vec0
\]
so \(\vec L\) is conserved. A fixed \(\vec L\) direction means \(\vec r\) and \(\vec v\) remain in the plane perpendicular to \(\vec L\), so the motion is planar.

questions.prompt: For a rigid body moving in a plane, derive \(L_O=\vec R_{\mathrm{cm}}\times M\vec V_{\mathrm{cm}}+I_{\mathrm{cm}}\omega\,\hat k\) about an arbitrary origin \(O\). State the condition under which the simpler form \(L_O=I_O\omega\) is valid.
questions.answer:
Write each particle position relative to the centre of mass:
\[
\vec r_i=\vec R_{\mathrm{cm}}+\vec\rho_i
\]
and velocity
\[
\vec v_i=\vec V_{\mathrm{cm}}+\vec\omega\times\vec\rho_i
\]
The angular momentum about \(O\) is
\[
\vec L_O=\sum_i \vec r_i\times m_i\vec v_i
\]
Substitute:
\[
\vec L_O=\sum_i(\vec R_{\mathrm{cm}}+\vec\rho_i)\times m_i(\vec V_{\mathrm{cm}}+\vec\omega\times\vec\rho_i)
\]
The centre-of-mass definitions give
\[
\sum_i m_i\vec\rho_i=\vec0
\]
so the mixed terms vanish. The result is
\[
\vec L_O=\vec R_{\mathrm{cm}}\times M\vec V_{\mathrm{cm}}+\sum_i\vec\rho_i\times m_i(\vec\omega\times\vec\rho_i)
\]
For planar rotation about a principal axis,
\[
\sum_i\vec\rho_i\times m_i(\vec\omega\times\vec\rho_i)=I_{\mathrm{cm}}\omega\,\hat k
\]
Thus
\[
L_O=\vec R_{\mathrm{cm}}\times M\vec V_{\mathrm{cm}}+I_{\mathrm{cm}}\omega\,\hat k
\]
The simpler form \(L_O=I_O\omega\) is valid when the body is in pure rotation about a fixed point or fixed axis through \(O\). It is not generally valid for a translating body.
